Bolli |url=https://www.itis.gov/servlet/SingleRpt/SingleRpt?search_topic=TSN&search_value=525079#null |website=ITIS Report |publisher=ITIS |access-date=13 July 2020}} }} '''''Sambucus canadensis''''', the '''American black elderberry''', '''Canada elderberry''', or '''common elderberry''', is a New World species of [[elderberry]] that forms a shrub primarily in [[temperate]] regions. Most parts of the plant are toxic with [[cyanogenic]] [[glycoside]]s, but the ripe berries can be cooked for food use with the seeds removed. ==Description== It is a [[deciduous]] suckering [[shrub]] growing to {{Convert|6|m|ft|abbr=off}} tall.{{cite web |title=NatureServe Explorer 2.0 - ''Sambucus nigra'' ssp. canadensis, Common Elderberry |url=https://explorer.natureserve.org/Taxon/ELEMENT_GLOBAL.2.638868/Sambucus_nigra_ssp_canadensis |website=explorer.natureserve.org |access-date=6 May 2020}}{{Cite book |title=The Complete Guide to Edible Wild Plants |publisher=[[Skyhorse Publishing]] |author=[[United States Department of the Army]] |year=2009 |isbn=978-1-60239-692-0 |location=New York |pages=53 |language=en-US |oclc=277203364}} The [[leaves]] are arranged in opposite pairs, pinnate with five to eleven leaflets, the leaflets averaging {{Convert|10|cm|abbr=off|frac=2}} long and 4 cm broad.{{cite book |last1=Niering |first1=William A. |author-link1=William Niering| last2=Olmstead |first2=Nancy C. |title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Wildflowers, Eastern Region |year=1985 |orig-year=1979|publisher=Knopf |isbn=0-394-50432-1 |page=448}} In summer, it bears large [[corymb]]s, {{Convert|20–30|cm|abbr=on|disp=or|frac=2}} diameter, of white [[flower]]s above the foliage, the individual flowers {{Convert|5–6|mm|frac=32}} diameter, with five petals.{{cite web |title=''Sambucus canadensis'' L., R. Bolli |url=https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Sambucus+canadensis|date=2026 |access-date=17 August 2026|website=Plants For A Future}} They are [[hermaphrodite]] and pollinated by insects. The [[fruit (botany)|fruit]] (known as an elderberry) is a dark purple to black [[berry (botany)|berry]] 3–5 mm diameter, produced in drooping clusters in the fall. {{gallery|mode=packed |Sambucus canadensis W IMG 3149.jpg|Foliage |Sambucus canadensis W IMG 3144.jpg|Flowers |Sambucus canadensis 004.JPG|Fruits }} ==Taxonomy== It is closely related to the European ''[[Sambucus nigra]]''. Some authors treat it as [[conspecific]], under the name ''Sambucus nigra'' subsp. ''canadensis''. ===Etymology=== The genus name comes from the Greek word ''sambuce'', an ancient wind instrument, in reference to the removal of pith from the twigs of this and other species to make whistles.{{cite book|last=Little|first=Elbert L.|title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Trees: Eastern Region|publisher=Knopf|location=New York|year=1980|isbn=0-394-50760-6|page=670}} ==Distribution and habitat== The species is native to a large area of North America east of the [[Rocky Mountains]], south throughout the mainland [[Americas]] to [[Bolivia]]. It is considered introduced in the Caribbean, Europe, Africa, and Asia.{{cite web |title=''Sambucus canadensis'' L. |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:321978-2 |publisher=Plants of the World Online, [[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]] |date=2026|access-date=6 June 2020}} ''S. canadensis'' is primarily found in habitat types such as marshes, swamps, and open woodland floodplains, among others.Weakley, A. S. (2015). ''Flora of the Southern and Mid-Atlantic States''. Chapel Hill, NC, University of North Carolina Herbarium. It grows in full sun to partial shade and can tolerate moist. sandy to clay soil with a medium [[Soil pH|pH]]. ==Toxicity== Inedible parts of the plant, such as the leaves, stems, roots, seeds and unripe fruits, can be toxic{{r|peterson1977}}{{cite book |last1=Preston | first1=Richard J. | last2=Braham | first2=Richard R. |date=2002 |title=North American Trees: Fifth Edition |location=Ames, Iowa|publisher=Iowa State Press |page=199 |isbn=0-8138-1526-6 }} due to the presence of cyanogenic glycosides and [[alkaloid]]s.{{cite web |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/sambucus-canadensis/ |title=''Sambucus canadensis'' |publisher=North Carolina State Extension Gardener|date=2026|access-date=24 July 2026}}{{cite web |vauthors=Oehler N, Waite-Cusic J, Hibbard-Swanson J |title=Play it safe when preserving elderberries |url=https://extension.oregonstate.edu/catalog/em-9446-play-it-safe-when-preserving-elderberries |publisher=Oregon State University Extension Service |access-date=24 July 2026 |date=November 2024}} ==Uses== Traditional methods of consuming elderberry includes sweetened jams, jellies, and syrups, all of which cook down the fruit and strain out the seeds.{{cite book |last=Peterson |first=Lee Allen |date=1977 |title=Edible Wild Plants: Eastern/Central North America |location=Boston|publisher=Houghton Mifflin Company |page=172 |isbn=0-395-92622-X }} A drink can be made from soaking the flower heads in water for eight hours. Other uses for the fruit include wine, jelly and dye. The leaves and inner bark may be used as an [[insecticide]] and a dye. The boiled inner bark of the elderberry was used by the [[Iroquois]] of North America as a [[pain reliever]] in [[toothache]]s, being applied to the side of the cheek that was most virulent.{{cite book|last=Kalm|first=Pehr|author-link=Pehr Kalm|title=Travels into North America |publisher=T. Lowndes |year=1772|location=London|translator=Johann Reinhold Forster |access-date=24 July 2026|url= https://archive.org/details/travelsintonorth01kalm_3/page/338/mode/1up|language=en|oclc=1083889360 }} ==References== {{Reflist}} {{Taxonbar|from=Q1640817}} [[Category:Sambucus|canadensis]] [[Category:Flora of Northern America]] [[Category:Flora of Southern America]] [[Category:Plants described in 1753]] [[Category:Botanical taxa named by Carl Linnaeus]] [[Category:Berries]] [[Category:Bird food plants]] [[Category:Edible plants]] [[Category:Medicinal plants of North America]]
